_readme: Additional species records (35) that complete the 48-species catalogue. Authored for this project from general knowledge of each species; each status is flagged as not re-checked against the live IUCN Red List (the build environment could not reach it). Population estimates are intentionally absent.

spoon-billed-sandpiper.name: Spoon-billed Sandpiper
spoon-billed-sandpiper.tagline: A tiny wader with a spoon-shaped bill that breeds in far-eastern Russia and winters on the coasts of South and Southeast Asia.
spoon-billed-sandpiper.summary: The spoon-billed sandpiper is a very small shorebird. Its spatula-tipped bill is used to sift mud and shallow water for food. Its survival depends on tidal mudflats in several countries, so protecting it means protecting a whole migration route.
spoon-billed-sandpiper.ecologicalRole: Forages on tidal mudflats for small invertebrates by sweeping its bill from side to side; it links Arctic breeding grounds with Asian coastal wetlands along a long migration route.
spoon-billed-sandpiper.habitat: Arctic coastal tundra (breeding) and tidal mudflats (non-breeding)
spoon-billed-sandpiper.region: Chukotka, Russia (breeding); coasts of Southeast Asia and Bangladesh (non-breeding)
threats: Loss of intertidal mudflats at migration stopovers
Trapping and hunting on wintering grounds
Disturbance and habitat change at breeding sites
conservationActions: International cooperation along the East Asian–Australasian Flyway
Captive-breeding and “head-starting” programmes that raise eggs and chicks for release
Work with local communities to reduce trapping on wintering grounds

audio.description: A short, high, soft trill suggesting a small wader
audio.hint: A synthesized high-pitched tone. It does not reproduce the bird’s real call.

whooping-crane.name: Whooping Crane
whooping-crane.tagline: North America’s tallest bird, whose only self-sustaining wild flock breeds in northern Canada and winters on the Texas coast.
whooping-crane.summary: Whooping cranes are tall white cranes with black wing tips. They were reduced to a very small number of birds in the twentieth century, and recovery has relied on long-term protection and captive breeding.
whooping-crane.ecologicalRole: An omnivorous wetland wader that eats crabs, clams, insects and plant matter in marshes and shallow water.
whooping-crane.habitat: Prairie and boreal wetlands (breeding); coastal salt marsh (winter)
whooping-crane.region: Wood Buffalo National Park, Canada (breeding) to the Texas Gulf Coast, USA (winter)

geo.locName: Aransas coast, Texas (wintering area, regional marker)

threats: Collisions with power lines and other structures
Loss and degradation of wetland habitat
Risk to a small, geographically concentrated wild flock from storms or spills
conservationActions: Habitat protection along the migration route

audio.description: A loud, trumpeting call suggesting a large crane
audio.hint: A synthesized low-mid tone. It does not reproduce the crane’s real call.

northern-bald-ibis.name: Northern Bald Ibis
northern-bald-ibis.tagline: A bald-headed, cliff-nesting ibis that once ranged across Europe, North Africa and the Middle East and now survives mainly in Morocco.
northern-bald-ibis.summary: The northern bald ibis has dark, glossy plumage, a bare red head and a long curved bill. It is highly social. Most wild birds now live in a few areas of Morocco, with managed groups elsewhere.
northern-bald-ibis.ecologicalRole: Forages in groups on dry ground for insects, lizards and other small animals, and nests in colonies on cliffs.
northern-bald-ibis.habitat: Semi-arid coastal and inland cliffs and open steppe
northern-bald-ibis.region: Morocco (main wild colonies); reintroduced groups in parts of Europe
threats: Loss of feeding habitat to development and tourism
conservationActions: Protection and wardening of wild colonies in Morocco
Reintroduction programmes, including guided migration, in Europe

audio.description: A hoarse, grunting call suggesting a colonial ibis
audio.hint: A synthesized mid tone. It does not reproduce the ibis’s real call.

african-penguin.name: African Penguin
african-penguin.tagline: A black-and-white seabird that breeds only on the coasts and islands of South Africa and Namibia.
african-penguin.summary: African penguins are medium-sized penguins with a black face band and pink skin patches above the eyes. They are also known as jackass penguins because of their donkey-like braying call. Their numbers have fallen steeply over recent decades.
african-penguin.ecologicalRole: Feeds on small schooling fish such as sardines and anchovies, so its breeding success is tied to the availability of that prey.
threats: Shortages of prey fish linked to fishing and shifting fish distributions
Warming seas and extreme weather affecting breeding
conservationActions: Fishing restrictions around some breeding colonies
Rescue, rehabilitation and hand-rearing of abandoned chicks and oiled birds
Artificial nests and predator management at colonies

audio.description: A braying call suggesting the “jackass” sound of this penguin
audio.hint: A synthesized bray-like tone. It does not reproduce the penguin’s real call.

shoebill.name: Shoebill
shoebill.tagline: A tall grey wetland bird with an enormous, shoe-shaped bill, found in the swamps of central and eastern Africa.
shoebill.summary: The shoebill stands over a metre tall and is known for its heavy bill, which it uses to grab large, slippery prey. It lives at low density in remote swamps and is sensitive to wetland loss and disturbance.
shoebill.ecologicalRole: An ambush predator that stands motionless in papyrus swamps and strikes at fish such as lungfish and catfish.
shoebill.region: South Sudan, Uganda, Zambia and neighbouring countries
threats: Disturbance, nest robbing and capture for the live-bird trade
Burning and grazing of wetland habitat
conservationActions: Wetland protection and community-based guiding at key sites
Monitoring and enforcement against capture and trade

audio.description: A bill-clattering sound suggesting a shoebill greeting display
audio.hint: A synthesized clatter-like tone. It does not reproduce the bird’s real bill-clattering.

komodo-dragon.name: Komodo Dragon
komodo-dragon.tagline: The heaviest living lizard, found on a handful of Indonesian islands.
komodo-dragon.summary: Komodo dragons are large monitor lizards with a strong sense of smell. Their entire range is a small group of islands, which makes them vulnerable to habitat change and sea-level rise.
komodo-dragon.ecologicalRole: A top predator of its islands that hunts deer and pigs and also scavenges carcasses.
komodo-dragon.habitat: Dry savanna, tropical dry forest and coastal areas
komodo-dragon.region: Komodo, Rinca, Flores and Gili Motang, Indonesia
threats: Rising sea levels projected to reduce suitable habitat
Human disturbance and illegal hunting of its prey
conservationActions: Monitoring of dragon and prey populations

audio.description: A low hiss suggesting a large monitor lizard
audio.hint: A synthesized hissing tone. It does not reproduce the lizard’s real hiss.

gharial.name: Gharial
gharial.tagline: A fish-eating crocodilian with a very long, narrow snout, restricted to a few rivers of the Indian subcontinent.
gharial.summary: The gharial’s slender snout is an adaptation for sweeping through water to catch fish. Adult males develop a bulb-like growth at the snout tip that amplifies a buzzing sound.
gharial.ecologicalRole: A specialist fish hunter whose presence reflects healthy river flow and undisturbed sandbanks for nesting.
gharial.region: Northern India and Nepal (remnant river populations)
threats: Dams, irrigation and sand mining that alter rivers and nesting banks
Entanglement and drowning in fishing nets

audio.description: A low buzzing hiss suggesting a gharial’s buzz
audio.hint: A synthesized buzzing tone. It does not reproduce the animal’s real sound.

chinese-alligator.name: Chinese Alligator
chinese-alligator.tagline: A small, armoured alligator that survives only in the lower Yangtze region of eastern China.
chinese-alligator.summary: Smaller than the American alligator, the Chinese alligator hibernates in burrows through winter. Its remaining wild habitat is a patchwork of small wetlands within farmland.
chinese-alligator.ecologicalRole: A burrowing predator of snails, fish and small animals whose burrows alter wetland habitat.
chinese-alligator.region: Anhui Province and neighbouring areas of eastern China
conservationActions: Captive breeding and release into protected areas

audio.description: A low bellow suggesting an alligator chorus
audio.hint: A synthesized low tone. It does not reproduce the alligator’s real bellow.

leatherback-turtle.name: Leatherback Sea Turtle

iucn.note: This is the global assessment. Several regional subpopulations are assessed in higher-risk categories.

leatherback-turtle.tagline: The largest living sea turtle, with a flexible, leathery shell and some of the longest migrations of any reptile.
leatherback-turtle.summary: Unlike other sea turtles, the leatherback has no hard shell plates. It dives deep and travels across entire ocean basins between feeding and nesting areas.
leatherback-turtle.ecologicalRole: Feeds mainly on jellyfish and other soft-bodied animals, which can help regulate their numbers.
leatherback-turtle.habitat: Open ocean; nests on tropical beaches
threats: Egg collection and loss of nesting beaches
Ingestion of plastic mistaken for jellyfish

audio.description: A heavy splash suggesting a large turtle surfacing
audio.hint: A synthesized splash-like tone. It is not an animal call.

green-sea-turtle.name: Green Sea Turtle

iucn.note: This is the global assessment. Status varies between regional subpopulations.

green-sea-turtle.tagline: A large, mostly herbivorous sea turtle found in tropical and subtropical seas worldwide.
green-sea-turtle.summary: The green turtle is named for the colour of its body fat, not its shell. It is one of the best-studied sea turtles, and its numbers differ greatly from region to region.
green-sea-turtle.ecologicalRole: Adults graze on seagrass and algae, which can help keep seagrass beds healthy; juveniles eat more animal prey.
green-sea-turtle.habitat: Seagrass meadows, coastal waters and nesting beaches

geo.locName: Caribbean coast of Costa Rica (representative nesting region)

threats: Harvest of eggs and turtles in some regions
Loss of nesting beaches and seagrass habitat
conservationActions: Legal protection and international trade controls

audio.description: A soft splash suggesting a turtle surfacing
audio.hint: A synthesized splash-like tone. It is not an animal call.

radiated-tortoise.name: Radiated Tortoise
radiated-tortoise.tagline: A strikingly patterned tortoise found only in the dry spiny forests of southern Madagascar.
radiated-tortoise.summary: Each scute of the radiated tortoise’s high, domed shell carries a star-like pattern of yellow lines. It lives only in a narrow region of Madagascar and is heavily targeted by illegal trade.
radiated-tortoise.ecologicalRole: A grazing herbivore that can spread plant seeds across spiny forest and scrub.
threats: Poaching for the illegal pet trade and for meat
Habitat loss to farming and charcoal production
conservationActions: Anti-trafficking enforcement and tortoise rescue centres
Captive breeding and release in some projects

audio.description: A low hiss suggesting a tortoise
audio.hint: A synthesized hissing tone. It is not a recording.

aldabra-giant-tortoise.name: Aldabra Giant Tortoise
aldabra-giant-tortoise.tagline: One of the world’s largest tortoises, living on Aldabra Atoll in the Seychelles, with managed groups on other islands.
aldabra-giant-tortoise.summary: The Aldabra giant tortoise grazes on grass and low plants and can live for many decades. Most of the world’s wild population lives on one remote atoll.
aldabra-giant-tortoise.ecologicalRole: A major grazer and seed disperser that shapes the vegetation of its island.
aldabra-giant-tortoise.habitat: Island grasslands, scrub and mangrove edges
aldabra-giant-tortoise.region: Aldabra Atoll, Seychelles (and introduced groups on other islands)
threats: Sea-level rise and extreme weather on low-lying atolls
Past harvest for meat and shells
conservationActions: Strict protection on Aldabra Atoll, a UNESCO World Heritage Site

audio.description: A deep hiss suggesting a very large tortoise
audio.hint: A synthesized hissing tone. It is not a recording.

chinese-giant-salamander.name: Chinese Giant Salamander

iucn.note: Genetic studies suggest this animal may be several species, which affects how its status is assessed.

chinese-giant-salamander.tagline: The world’s largest amphibian, a fully aquatic salamander of cool, clear mountain streams in China.
chinese-giant-salamander.summary: This giant salamander has wrinkled skin and tiny eyes and hunts mainly at night by sensing movement in the water. Wild populations have fallen sharply; many animals in farms are not suitable for release.
chinese-giant-salamander.ecologicalRole: An ambush predator of fish, crustaceans and other prey in clean, fast streams.
chinese-giant-salamander.habitat: Cool, clear mountain streams and caves
threats: Harvest for food and traditional uses
Pollution and degradation of stream habitat
conservationActions: Captive breeding and release trials with attention to genetics

audio.description: A low gurgle suggesting a large aquatic salamander
audio.hint: A synthesized gurgling tone. The animal is known for faint sounds only.

golden-poison-frog.name: Golden Poison Frog
golden-poison-frog.tagline: A small, brightly coloured rainforest frog from the Pacific lowlands of Colombia that carries powerful skin toxins.
golden-poison-frog.summary: The golden poison frog’s bright colour is a warning to predators. It lives in a small patch of rainforest, so local forest loss matters a great deal for the whole species.
golden-poison-frog.ecologicalRole: A leaf-litter insect eater. Its skin toxins are thought to come from its diet in the wild.

audio.description: A short, high trill suggesting a small frog
audio.hint: A synthesized trill-like tone. It does not reproduce the frog’s real call.

panamanian-golden-frog.name: Panamanian Golden Frog

iucn.note: Its status in the wild is uncertain; check the latest assessment.

panamanian-golden-frog.tagline: A bright yellow harlequin toad that is a national symbol of Panama and survives mainly in captive assurance colonies.
panamanian-golden-frog.summary: The Panamanian golden frog communicates partly with hand waves, an adaptation to noisy streams. Chytrid fungus has devastated many amphibians worldwide, and this species is a well-known example.
panamanian-golden-frog.ecologicalRole: A stream-side insect eater and a flagship for amphibian conservation and for the fight against chytrid disease.
threats: Past collection for the pet trade
conservationActions: Captive assurance colonies in Panama and abroad
Research on chytrid disease and treatments

audio.description: A faint chirp suggesting a small toad
audio.hint: A synthesized chirp-like tone. The species is known for visual signalling, not loud calls.

goliath-frog.name: Goliath Frog
goliath-frog.tagline: The largest living frog, found in fast-flowing rivers of Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea.
goliath-frog.summary: Goliath frogs can be much larger than other frogs and lay eggs in rocky, flowing water. They have no vocal sac and are rarely heard.
goliath-frog.ecologicalRole: A large predator and prey item in river ecosystems that is sensitive to river quality.
goliath-frog.habitat: Fast-flowing, clear rainforest rivers and waterfalls
conservationActions: Protected areas in parts of its range
Research on breeding and habitat needs

audio.description: A low gurgle suggesting a very large frog
audio.hint: A synthesized tone. This frog has no vocal sac and is mostly silent, so the sound is purely illustrative.

lake-titicaca-frog.name: Lake Titicaca Frog
lake-titicaca-frog.tagline: A wrinkle-skinned, fully aquatic frog that lives only in Lake Titicaca and nearby waters on the Peru–Bolivia border.
lake-titicaca-frog.summary: The frog’s baggy skin increases the surface for taking in oxygen. It is entirely aquatic and rarely comes to the surface.
lake-titicaca-frog.ecologicalRole: Absorbs oxygen through loose skin folds in the cold, high-altitude lake and is an indicator of lake health.
conservationActions: Legal protection and enforcement against harvest

audio.description: A soft gurgle suggesting an underwater frog
audio.hint: A synthesized gurgling tone. It is not a recording.

darwins-frog.name: Darwin’s Frog
darwins-frog.tagline: A small, leaf-mimicking frog of Chile and Argentina whose males carry developing tadpoles in their vocal sacs.
darwins-frog.summary: Darwin’s frog has a pointed snout and leaf-like shape. Males keep tadpoles in their vocal sac until they develop into froglets.
darwins-frog.ecologicalRole: A small insect-eater of cool, humid forest leaf litter.
conservationActions: Protected areas in Chile and Argentina

audio.description: A short, high whistle suggesting a small forest frog
audio.hint: A synthesized whistle-like tone. It does not reproduce the frog’s real call.

purple-frog.name: Purple Frog
purple-frog.tagline: A burrowing, pig-snouted frog of India’s Western Ghats that spends most of its life underground.
purple-frog.summary: The purple frog has a round, bloated body and a small, pointed head. It belongs to an ancient family found only in India and Sri Lanka and was formally described in 2003.
purple-frog.ecologicalRole: Feeds on termites underground and emerges briefly during the monsoon to breed.
purple-frog.habitat: Moist forest soils and streams of the Western Ghats
threats: Habitat fragmentation by roads and development
conservationActions: Protection of key habitat in the Western Ghats

audio.description: A low call suggesting a burrowing frog
audio.hint: A synthesized low tone. It does not reproduce the frog’s real call.

whale-shark.name: Whale Shark
whale-shark.tagline: The largest living fish, a slow-moving filter feeder of tropical seas.
whale-shark.summary: The whale shark is a shark, not a whale. It has a wide mouth and a spotted pattern that is unique to each animal.
whale-shark.ecologicalRole: Filters plankton and small fish from the water, moving long distances between feeding areas.
whale-shark.habitat: Tropical and warm-temperate open ocean and coasts
conservationActions: Listing on CITES Appendix II and national protection
Codes of conduct for wildlife tourism

audio.description: A very low tone suggesting a huge, slow animal
audio.hint: Not a recording and not an animal call: this species is not known for making sounds, so the tone is purely illustrative.

great-white-shark.name: Great White Shark
great-white-shark.tagline: A large apex predator of temperate and subtropical seas that travels along coasts and across open ocean.
great-white-shark.summary: Great white sharks grow slowly, mature late and produce few young, so populations recover slowly after losses.
great-white-shark.ecologicalRole: A top predator that preys on seals, fish and other marine animals.
threats: Shark control programmes and the shark-fin trade in some regions
Slow growth and late maturity, which slow recovery

audio.description: A very low tone suggesting a large predator
audio.hint: Not a recording and not an animal call: this species is not known for making sounds, so the tone is purely illustrative.

european-eel.name: European Eel
european-eel.tagline: A snake-like migratory fish that is born in the Sargasso Sea, grows in European rivers and returns to the ocean to spawn.
european-eel.summary: European eels make one of the longest migrations of any freshwater fish. Their spawning has never been directly observed, which makes protection difficult.
european-eel.ecologicalRole: A predator and scavenger in rivers and estuaries that links ocean and freshwater systems.
european-eel.habitat: Rivers, lakes, estuaries and the Sargasso Sea (spawning)
european-eel.region: Europe, North Africa and the Atlantic (spawning in the Sargasso Sea)
threats: Dams, pumps and other barriers that block migration
Overfishing, including of young glass eels, and illegal trade
conservationActions: Eel management plans and fishing limits in the European Union
Trade restrictions under CITES Appendix II

audio.description: A faint gurgle suggesting a river fish
audio.hint: Not a recording and not an animal call: this species is not known for making sounds, so the tone is purely illustrative.

beluga-sturgeon.name: Beluga Sturgeon
beluga-sturgeon.tagline: A giant, long-lived fish of the Caspian and Black Sea basins, known for the caviar made from its eggs.
beluga-sturgeon.summary: Beluga sturgeons are among the largest freshwater and migratory fish. They mature late, so overfishing has long-lasting effects.
beluga-sturgeon.ecologicalRole: A large predatory fish that migrates upriver to spawn.
beluga-sturgeon.habitat: Seas, large rivers and spawning grounds
beluga-sturgeon.region: Caspian Sea, Black Sea and Adriatic basins; spawning rivers such as the Volga and Ural
conservationActions: Trade controls on caviar under CITES (all sturgeons are listed)

audio.description: A low tone suggesting a very large river fish
audio.hint: Not a recording and not an animal call: this species is not known for making sounds, so the tone is purely illustrative.

humphead-wrasse.name: Humphead Wrasse

taxonomy.note: Some classifications place wrasses in the order Perciformes.

humphead-wrasse.tagline: A very large coral-reef fish with a prominent forehead hump, also called the Napoleon wrasse.
humphead-wrasse.summary: Humphead wrasses can live for decades and change sex during their lives. They are heavily targeted for the luxury live-fish trade.
humphead-wrasse.ecologicalRole: Eats hard-shelled invertebrates and also crown-of-thorns starfish, a species that can damage coral.
humphead-wrasse.region: Indo-Pacific reefs from the Red Sea to the central Pacific
threats: Overfishing for the live reef-fish trade
conservationActions: Size and catch limits in some countries

audio.description: A soft bubbling tone suggesting a reef fish
audio.hint: Not a recording and not an animal call: this species is not known for making sounds, so the tone is purely illustrative.

smalltooth-sawfish.name: Smalltooth Sawfish
smalltooth-sawfish.tagline: A ray with a long, toothed snout that was once common in coastal waters of the Atlantic and is now rare across much of its range.
smalltooth-sawfish.summary: Sawfishes are rays, not sharks. The saw is covered with sensors and is also used to stun prey.
smalltooth-sawfish.ecologicalRole: Uses its toothed snout to sense and strike prey in shallow coastal water and estuaries.
smalltooth-sawfish.habitat: Shallow coastal waters, estuaries and river mouths
smalltooth-sawfish.region: Atlantic coasts; its main remaining stronghold in the USA is in Florida
threats: Loss of mangrove and estuarine nursery habitat
conservationActions: Legal protection, including under the US Endangered Species Act
Guidelines for safe release of accidental catches

audio.description: A short click suggesting a fish-like sound
audio.hint: Not a recording and not an animal call: this species is not known for making sounds, so the tone is purely illustrative.

mekong-giant-catfish.name: Mekong Giant Catfish
mekong-giant-catfish.tagline: One of the world’s largest freshwater fish, which migrates along the Mekong River system.
mekong-giant-catfish.summary: The Mekong giant catfish is scaleless and can grow very large. Its numbers have fallen sharply because it depends on a free-flowing river for migration.
mekong-giant-catfish.ecologicalRole: A large river fish that feeds mainly on algae and plant material as an adult and migrates to spawn.
threats: Changes to river flow and habitat
conservationActions: Fishing restrictions in parts of its range

audio.description: A low tone suggesting a very large river fish
audio.hint: Not a recording and not an animal call: this species is not known for making sounds, so the tone is purely illustrative.

lined-seahorse.name: Lined Seahorse
lined-seahorse.tagline: A seahorse of Atlantic coastal waters, in which the male carries the eggs in a brood pouch.
lined-seahorse.summary: Seahorses are fish with a tail that can grip seagrass. Males give birth to the young, which are not cared for after birth.
lined-seahorse.ecologicalRole: An ambush feeder on small crustaceans among seagrass and reef structures.
lined-seahorse.habitat: Seagrass beds, reefs and coastal waters
lined-seahorse.region: Western Atlantic from Canada to the Caribbean and South America
threats: Harvest for traditional medicine, the aquarium trade and curios
conservationActions: Listing of all seahorses on CITES Appendix II

audio.description: A faint clicking suggesting a seahorse’s feeding click
audio.hint: A synthesized click-like tone. It is not a recording.

monarch-butterfly.name: Monarch Butterfly

iucn.note: The Endangered assessment applies to the migratory subspecies (Danaus plexippus plexippus) of North America. The species as a whole is a different case.

monarch-butterfly.tagline: An orange-and-black butterfly whose North American populations migrate thousands of kilometres each year.
monarch-butterfly.summary: No single monarch makes the full round trip. It takes several generations to complete the annual migration cycle.
monarch-butterfly.ecologicalRole: Adults pollinate flowers; caterpillars feed only on milkweed plants.
monarch-butterfly.region: North America: breeding across the USA and Canada; overwintering in Mexico and California

geo.locName: Monarch Butterfly Biosphere Reserve, Mexico (overwintering area)

threats: Loss of milkweed and nectar plants
conservationActions: Protection of overwintering forests in Mexico

audio.description: A soft flutter-like tone suggesting wings
audio.hint: Not a recording and not an animal call: this species is not known for making sounds, so the tone is purely illustrative.

lord-howe-stick-insect.name: Lord Howe Island Stick Insect
lord-howe-stick-insect.tagline: A large, flightless stick insect once thought extinct and rediscovered on a sea stack near Lord Howe Island.
lord-howe-stick-insect.summary: The stick insect was feared extinct after rats reached the island in the early twentieth century. It was found again in 2001 on Ball’s Pyramid.
lord-howe-stick-insect.ecologicalRole: A nocturnal plant-eater that was once common on Lord Howe Island before introduced rats arrived.
lord-howe-stick-insect.habitat: Shrubland on Ball’s Pyramid; formerly forest on Lord Howe Island
lord-howe-stick-insect.region: Ball’s Pyramid and Lord Howe Island, Australia
threats: Introduced black rats, the historical cause of its loss from the main island
conservationActions: A captive-breeding programme at Melbourne Zoo
A rodent-removal programme on Lord Howe Island intended to allow future reintroduction

audio.description: A faint rustle suggesting an insect
audio.hint: Not a recording and not an animal call: this species is not known for making sounds, so the tone is purely illustrative.

staghorn-coral.name: Staghorn Coral
staghorn-coral.tagline: A branching reef-building coral of the Caribbean and western Atlantic, once among the most abundant on shallow reefs.
staghorn-coral.summary: Staghorn coral grows quickly, and fragments can regrow, which is why restoration programmes use nurseries. It is a coral animal colony with algae living in its tissue.
staghorn-coral.ecologicalRole: Builds reef structure that shelters fish and invertebrates and helps protect coasts.
staghorn-coral.region: Caribbean Sea, Gulf of Mexico and western Atlantic
conservationActions: Coral nurseries that grow fragments for outplanting

audio.description: A soft bubbling tone suggesting a reef soundscape
audio.hint: Not a recording and not an animal call: this species is not known for making sounds, so the tone is purely illustrative.

elkhorn-coral.name: Elkhorn Coral
elkhorn-coral.tagline: A large, flattened-branch coral that forms the shallow, wave-facing crest of many Caribbean reefs.
elkhorn-coral.summary: Elkhorn coral looks like the antlers of an elk. Its numbers fell steeply from the 1980s onward, mainly because of disease and warming.
elkhorn-coral.ecologicalRole: Its thick branches absorb wave energy, which helps protect shorelines and shelters reef animals.
elkhorn-coral.region: Caribbean Sea, Gulf of Mexico and western Atlantic
threats: Disease outbreaks, such as white-band disease
conservationActions: Legal protection, including under the US Endangered Species Act

audio.description: A soft bubbling tone suggesting a reef soundscape
audio.hint: Not a recording and not an animal call: this species is not known for making sounds, so the tone is purely illustrative.

queen-alexandras-birdwing.name: Queen Alexandra’s Birdwing
queen-alexandras-birdwing.tagline: The world’s largest butterfly, found only in a small area of lowland rainforest in Papua New Guinea.
queen-alexandras-birdwing.summary: Females can have a wingspan of over 25 centimetres. The species lives in a very small range, so forest clearing there has a large effect.
queen-alexandras-birdwing.ecologicalRole: Its caterpillars depend on a particular group of vines, so the butterfly is tied to specific forest plants.

geo.locName: Oro Province, Papua New Guinea (regional marker)

threats: Forest clearing, including for oil-palm plantations
Volcanic eruptions in its small range
conservationActions: Legal protection in Papua New Guinea
Forest conservation and community butterfly projects

audio.description: A soft flutter-like tone suggesting large wings
audio.hint: Not a recording and not an animal call: this species is not known for making sounds, so the tone is purely illustrative.

giant-clam.name: Giant Clam

taxonomy.note: Some classifications place this family in the order Venerida.

giant-clam.tagline: The largest living bivalve, which hosts algae in its tissues and lives on shallow Indo-Pacific reefs.
giant-clam.summary: A giant clam can live for decades and its colourful mantle contains algae. It is farmed in hatcheries to supply restocking and the aquarium trade.
giant-clam.ecologicalRole: Filters water and gets part of its energy from symbiotic algae; its shell shelters other reef animals.
threats: Overharvest for meat and the shell trade
conservationActions: Listing of giant clams on CITES Appendix II

audio.description: A soft bubbling tone suggesting a reef soundscape
audio.hint: Not a recording and not an animal call: this species is not known for making sounds, so the tone is purely illustrative.

american-horseshoe-crab.name: Atlantic Horseshoe Crab

taxonomy.note: Horseshoe crabs are marine arthropods more closely related to spiders and scorpions than to crabs.

american-horseshoe-crab.tagline: An ancient-looking marine arthropod that comes ashore to spawn on Atlantic beaches.
american-horseshoe-crab.summary: Horseshoe crab blood is used to test medical products for bacterial contamination, so some animals are caught, bled and released.
american-horseshoe-crab.ecologicalRole: Its eggs are an important food for migrating shorebirds such as the red knot.
american-horseshoe-crab.habitat: Shallow coastal waters, estuaries and spawning beaches
american-horseshoe-crab.region: Atlantic coast of North America and the Gulf of Mexico
threats: Harvest for bait and for biomedical use
Loss of spawning beaches to development and erosion
conservationActions: Catch limits and bait quotas set by states
Development of synthetic alternatives to blood-based tests

audio.description: A faint clicking suggesting a shelled animal on sand
audio.hint: Not a recording and not an animal call: this species is not known for making sounds, so the tone is purely illustrative.

tasmanian-giant-crayfish.name: Tasmanian Giant Freshwater Crayfish
tasmanian-giant-crayfish.tagline: The world’s largest freshwater invertebrate, living in rivers of northern Tasmania.
tasmanian-giant-crayfish.summary: The Tasmanian giant freshwater crayfish grows slowly and breeds late in life, so it recovers slowly from losses of adults or habitat.
tasmanian-giant-crayfish.ecologicalRole: Feeds on decaying wood and leaves, recycling nutrients in streams.
tasmanian-giant-crayfish.habitat: Cool, clear rivers in forested catchments
threats: Clearing of streamside forest and sedimentation
conservationActions: Legal protection, including a ban on taking the species

audio.description: A faint clicking suggesting a crayfish
audio.hint: Not a recording and not an animal call: this species is not known for making sounds, so the tone is purely illustrative.
